title: Secondary School Teachers
text:
These resources aren’t just for university classrooms. You’re more than welcome to bring them into your own secondary school teaching. Most of the hooks and activities on this site come with self-guided instructions, so you can pick one up, adapt it to your year level, and run it with minimal preparation. If you’d like a bit more support getting started, though, I’m happy to run a training session or professional development day for your staff, whether that’s a hands-on walkthrough of specific activities, or a broader conversation about building this kind of engagement-first approach into your own teaching.
I also offer free live talks in schools, mainly around the Melbourne (Australia) area. These sessions cover why maths, statistics, and data science actually matter, not in an abstract “it’s important” sense, but through real activities, real jobs, and honest conversations about where the field is heading, including AI (and why I’m not particularly worried about it). I run students through some of the same kinds of hooks featured on this site, talk about the career paths these skills open up, and try to leave them with a genuinely different picture of what statistics and data science look like in practice. Talks are fully customisable to different year levels, from junior secondary through to senior students starting to think about post-school options.
This is something I offer freely, as part of my role as Deputy Director of Engagement. I think engaging with schools and the wider community is one of the most valuable things a university can do, not just as outreach, but as a genuine two-way relationship. Students get exposure to ideas and pathways they might not otherwise encounter, and in turn, it keeps me grounded in what actually resonates with a room full of teenagers, which shapes how I think about teaching more broadly.
If a training session, PD day, or school talk sounds like something your school would be interested in, please get in touch at minh.huynh1@monash.edu. Let me know your year level, group size, and what you’re hoping to get out of it, and we can figure out the right format together.

title: The Witness Test
text: Eyewitness Memory Overconfidence Calibration Uncertainty

title: The Witness Test
text:
About
This app puts students in the position of an eyewitness. They watch a short 15-second animated crime scene, then answer 10 multiple-choice questions about what they saw — rating their confidence alongside each answer. The gap between confidence and accuracy is the whole point: students are almost always more sure of themselves than their actual scores justify, mirroring a well-documented finding in eyewitness testimony research. This is a great entry point for discussing calibration (does 80% confidence really mean 80% correct?), the reliability of eyewitness evidence in legal contexts, and how overconfidence can quietly distort real-world decision-making even when someone feels certain.

title: The Witness Test
text:
General questions

Before seeing your score, how confident were you overall that you’d remembered the scene accurately? Did your actual score match that feeling?
Were there any specific questions where you felt very confident but got the answer wrong? What might explain that gap?
Does higher confidence always mean higher accuracy? Based on your own results, what would you say the relationship actually looks like?
If a real eyewitness tells police “I’m 100% sure that’s the person I saw,” should that statement alone be treated as strong evidence? Why or why not?
What factors do you think affect how well someone remembers a brief, stressful event — and were any of those factors present (or missing) in this 15-second clip?
As a class, compare everyone’s confidence-vs-accuracy patterns. Does everyone show the same overconfidence pattern, or do some people seem better calibrated than others?
Courts often rely heavily on eyewitness testimony, sometimes as the primary piece of evidence in a case. Based on this activity, what changes (if any) do you think should be made to how eyewitness evidence is used or presented in trials?
Outside of courtrooms, where else in life might overconfidence in your own memory or judgment cause problems, even when you feel completely certain?

title: The Stolen Laptop
text: Bayesian Inference Prior & Posterior Beta Distribution Sequential Updating

title: The Stolen Laptop
text:
About
This app puts students in the role of a judge in a Bayesian courtroom. Minh is on trial for stealing a laptop, and students start with a completely uninformative prior — a flat Beta(1, 1) distribution over the probability of guilt. Across 8 rounds, the prosecution and defence alternate presenting pieces of evidence, and after each one, students rate how strongly it points toward guilt or innocence on a 0–10 slider. That rating is converted into binomial-style evidence and used to update the posterior distribution — which then becomes the prior for the next round. By the end, students can see the full sequence of distributions stacked as a ridge plot, watching the belief about Minh’s guilt sharpen (or shift) with every new piece of evidence. This is a concrete, visual way to teach Bayesian updating as an iterative process rather than a single formula — and a good opportunity to discuss how much any one juror’s subjective rating of “how strong is this evidence” ends up steering the entire final verdict.

General questions

Why does the app start with a Beta(1, 1) prior instead of, say, assuming Minh is 50% likely to be guilty from the outset? What does a “flat” prior actually represent?
After the very first piece of evidence, how much did the posterior mean shift? Did it feel proportional to how strongly you rated that evidence?
The posterior from one round becomes the prior for the next. Why does this sequential updating process make sense, rather than treating each piece of evidence completely independently?
If two different students rated the exact same piece of evidence very differently on the slider, would they end up with different final verdicts? What does that tell you about the role of subjective judgement in this model?
Look at the ridge plot at the end. Does the distribution get narrower (more confident) or wider (less confident) as more evidence comes in? Why would that happen either way?
If the very last piece of evidence were extremely strong, would it “erase” everything the earlier evidence suggested, or does it just nudge the existing posterior? Why?
Real juries don’t use sliders and formal posterior distributions, but arguably do something similar in their heads. What are the risks of that being done informally rather than explicitly, the way this app forces you to?
If the order of evidence presentation were shuffled (defence evidence first, prosecution last, etc.), would you expect the final posterior to end up the same? Why or why not?

title: The Life Ledger
text: Survival Analysis Hazard Function Survival Curve Competing Risks

title: The Life Ledger
text:
About
This app turns survival analysis into a life-simulation game. Students first choose between two difficulty settings — Standard Mode, representing a well-resourced setting with strong healthcare, education, and social safety nets, or Hard Mode, representing a low-resource setting where the same choices carry far more risk — before allocating a fixed budget of points across five life traits: Health, Fitness, Intelligence, Discipline, and Social. These shape three emergent traits (Vitality, Happiness, Risk) that students don’t control directly. From there, students simulate their character year by year, watching age-appropriate life events unfold — school, then work or study, with a chance of marriage and kids along the way (weighted by Social and Happiness) — while a hazard function recalculates their odds of death every year from natural ageing risk, accident risk, and freak-chance risk. Every decade guarantees two positive events (shown in green) and two negative events (shown in red), with negative events escalating to hospitalizations or mental-health crises if Health or Social drop too low — and those, in turn, substantially raise the character’s ongoing risk of death.
At the end of each life, students get a comparable Life Score and a short written summary of how that life went. The two modes are calibrated very differently: in Standard Mode, dying before 60 is engineered to be extremely rare (under a 1-in-1000 chance for a typically-played character), while in Hard Mode it’s far more common and much more sensitive to neglecting Health and Fitness early on — making the two modes a natural pair to compare side by side.

Look at your final Life Score. What does it actually reward — longevity, well-rounded stats, life events, or some mix? Do you think it’s measuring the “right” things, or would you weight it differently?
If you ran the same trait allocation through Hard Mode ten times, would you expect wildly different outcomes each time, or fairly similar ones? What does that suggest about how much of a life’s length is “luck” versus “choices” in this model?
Compare your Standard Mode life summary to your Hard Mode one side by side. Beyond just the age at death, what else changed about the shape of the two lives?

title: Box Office Model Builder
text: Multiple Regression Variable Selection Omitted Variable Bias Model Fit

title: Box Office Model Builder
text:
About
This app puts students in the seat of a data analyst pitching a box office model. Students first choose exactly 3 predictors — from a pool of 23 candidate variables, roughly half genuinely related to box office and half mostly noise — and fit a real OLS regression on 200 synthetic past films, complete with coefficients, standard errors, t-statistics, p-values, R², adjusted R², and RMSE. Then the twist: an “executive” insists on adding 3 more variables, and students must allocate a fixed £100m budget across all 6 fields before the true (previously hidden) box office outcome is revealed. The gap between the student’s 3-variable prediction and the revealed truth is a direct, visual lesson in omitted variable bias — a model can look statistically solid and still be badly wrong if it’s missing the variables that actually matter. The budget stage adds a second layer: since real investment is modelled to genuinely shift outcomes (with diminishing returns), students also see the consequence of spreading money across variables that don’t actually move the needle versus committing to the ones that do.

General questions

Before seeing the regression output, how did you decide which 3 variables to pick? Did your reasoning match what the p-values and R² ended up showing?
Two students could pick 3 completely different variables and both get a “significant” model (low p-values). Does statistical significance alone tell you whether a model is actually good? What else would you want to check?
Your R² was well below 1, even with genuinely strong predictors. Why would a regression using real, meaningful variables still leave a lot of variation unexplained?
When the executive added 3 more variables, did you already suspect what kind of variables they might be? How did seeing them change your view of your original model?
If your final prediction was way off from the true outcome, was that because your original 3 variables were poorly chosen, or because any 3-variable model was always going to miss something? How would you tell the difference?
In the budget stage, did you spread your £100m evenly, or concentrate it on a few fields? Looking back, would a different allocation have changed the final outcome much?
If you allocated a large chunk of budget to one of the executive’s added variables and it barely moved the outcome, what does that tell you about the difference between a variable being included in a budget decision versus a variable actually driving the result?
In the real film industry, studios spend heavily on data and market research before greenlighting a movie. Based on this activity, what’s the risk of trusting a model that only includes 3 or 4 variables, even if it looks statistically strong?

title: World Cup Simulator
text: Likelihood Simulation Monte Carlo Methods Probability Models

title: World Cup Simulator
text:
About
This app simulates a full 32-team knockout World Cup bracket across three tabs of increasing sophistication. The 50/50 bracket tab (tab 1) runs the tournament with every match decided by a coin flip, letting students see how the bracket structure itself works and how much randomness alone can produce a “surprise” champion. The Custom probabilities tab (tab 2) hands control to the students — before each match, they set the probability that the higher-seeded team wins, immediately turning an abstract “likelihood” into something they’re directly manipulating and watching play out. The Team strengths tab is the main event: students assign a strength rating (0–100) to every team, the app converts each pair of ratings into a match-win probability, and then runs the entire tournament hundreds or thousands of times, tallying how often each team reaches each stage. This is a hands-on introduction to likelihood-based modelling — students aren’t just predicting a single outcome, they’re defining the probability model itself, then using repeated simulation to see what that model implies about the full range of possible tournaments.

General questions

In the 50/50 bracket, does a team’s path through the draw (who they happen to face each round) matter at all, given every match is a coin flip? Why might a “weak” team still end up champion sometimes?
On the Custom probabilities tab, if you set every match to 70% in favour of the stronger team, does that guarantee the stronger team wins the tournament? What does “70% per match” actually compound into across 5 rounds?
On the Team strengths tab, two teams rated 80 and 20 face off. Roughly what does the model say their win probability split should be, and does that feel fair given the 4x difference in rating?
Why does running the simulation 1000 times give you a very different (and more useful) picture than running it just once, even though the underlying probability model hasn’t changed at all?
If your favourite team wins the “Champion” column only 15 times out of 1000 simulations, does that mean the model thinks they’re unlikely to win, or does 15/1000 still represent a real chance? How would you explain that number to someone who’s never seen a simulation like this before?
The strength ratings you assign are essentially a guess. How would you go about testing whether your ratings are actually reasonable, using real-world information about the teams?
What’s the difference between the probability the model assigns to a team winning a single match, and the likelihood of that team ending up champion after 5 rounds? Why aren’t these the same number?

title: Should We Launch It?
text: Bayesian Inference Beta-Binomial Model Conjugate Priors Sequential Updating

title: Should We Launch It?
text:
About
This app is a companion piece to The Stolen Laptop, but framed around a business decision instead of a courtroom: should a café launch a new product, based on customer feedback? Students start with a flat Beta(1, 1) prior on the true proportion of customers who genuinely support the launch. Over 6 simulated days, a fresh batch of customer comments arrives each day, and students read through them, checking off which ones they judge as genuine support. That count (say, 6 out of 10 comments) is treated as binomial data and combined with the current prior using the conjugate beta-binomial update: \(\alpha \to \alpha + x\), \(\beta \to \beta + (n - x)\). Because the update rule is just simple addition, this is a great follow-up to the courtroom app for showing students why the beta distribution is used as a prior for proportions in the first place — the math is transparent enough to do by hand, while the app’s ridge plot makes the accumulating evidence visually obvious. The app also lets students copy the day-by-day data directly into R, to double-check the same result using dbeta() or a package like bayesrules.

title: Should We Launch It?
text:
General questions

Why is Beta(1, 1) a sensible “starting point” if you genuinely have no idea whether customers support the launch? What would it mean to start with a different prior instead, like Beta(10, 10) or Beta(2, 8)?
The update rule is just \(\alpha \to \alpha + x\) and \(\beta \to \beta + (n - x)\). Why does adding the count of “genuine support” comments to \(\alpha\), and the count of the rest to \(\beta\), make sense conceptually?
Does the order in which the 6 days of feedback arrive change the final posterior? Try to reason through this without running the app again — would summing everything at once give the same answer as updating day by day?
After 6 days, is the posterior distribution narrower or wider than the Day 1 posterior? What does that tell you about how confident you should be by the end?
If Day 1 had unusually strong support (say, 9 out of 10 comments) purely by chance, how much does that early result continue to influence the final posterior after 5 more days of data? Does its influence shrink over time?
How is this beta-binomial setup similar to the courtroom app’s evidence-rating process? How is it different — specifically, which one relies on a subjective 0–10 rating, and which one relies on a countable, objective tally?
If you were the café owner, at what posterior mean (or what width of posterior distribution) would you feel comfortable actually launching the product? Is there a “right” threshold, or is that a business judgement call layered on top of the statistics?
The app lets you copy the daily counts into R. Why might it be useful to double-check an app’s calculations independently, rather than just trusting the visual output?

title: About
text:
This site is a collection of statistical hooks - quick, memorable ways to open a topic, grab attention, and make an abstract concept feel concrete before you dive into the technical details. The idea is simple:

if you can hook students’ curiosity early, you can hold their attention longer once the harder explanations start.
They also work well as a reset: a way to re-energise the room after wrapping up a dense topic, before moving on to the next.

The resource is currently split into two main sections, with a third on the way.
Demonstration Hooks are designed for larger classes, like lectures, where the instructor leads the activity (think a card trick, a rigged coin flip, or a jar of lollies passed around the room). These work well as a live, front-of-room demonstration: you’re doing the trick, and the class is watching, guessing, and reacting together. They’re a great way to open a lecture or transition between topics without needing every student to have a device in hand.
Interactive Hooks flip the above dynamic. Students engage directly with an app or activity themselves, often game-like in nature. These can still work in a lecture setting, but I’ve mostly used them in smaller classes, like tutorials, where everyone can get hands-on. Many include a built-in scoring system, and students genuinely respond to that competitive edge — it’s a small addition that adds a surprising amount of engagement.
A third section, Stories, is coming soon — a collection of interesting real-world stories you can bring into class to illustrate statistical ideas in action.

title: Stacked Deck
text: Hypothesis Testing Null vs Alternative Type I Error Probability

title: Stacked Deck
text:
About
This activity uses a fully controlled card trick to walk students through five hypothesis tests in a row, live. Before class, the instructor writes down five pairs of hypotheses and secretly stacks the deck so that, one at a time, each “rare” alternative outcome is forced to occur. Because the audience believes the cards are shuffled randomly, each reveal looks like a genuinely surprising result — which is exactly the intuition hypothesis testing is built on: if the null were true, this outcome would almost never happen, so something else must be going on.

title: Stacked Deck
text: Demonstration

title: Stacked Deck
text:
Materials

A standard deck of 52 playing cards, pre-arranged in advance (see Pre-tasks)
5 printed or written prediction cards/slides, sealed or hidden until each reveal
A table or document camera so the class can see the cards clearly
A whiteboard or slide to record each hypothesis pair and the outcome

title: Stacked Deck
text:
The Five Predictions
Write these down and seal them before class. Rewritten slightly below for statistical clarity — feel free to adjust wording to match your own phrasing style.








#
\(H_0\) (expected / common)
\(H_1\) (rare / alternative)




1
The number of face-up cards will equal the number of face-down cards
The number of face-up cards will be less than the number of face-down cards


2
Of the remaining cards, there will be a mix of number cards and picture cards
Of the remaining cards, there will be number cards only


3
Of the remaining cards, there will be a mix of red and black cards
Of the remaining cards, there will be exactly 10 black cards


4
Of those 10 black cards, there will be a mix of spades and clubs
Of those 10 black cards, there will be clubs only


5
—
The one black card that isn’t a club is the Ace of Spades









How the trick works





The entire deck is pre-arranged before class using a false shuffle (a shuffle that looks random but preserves a known order) combined with cards deliberately mixed face-up and face-down in a controlled pattern. Because the final arrangement is fully known in advance, each “surprising” outcome — fewer face-up cards, only number cards remaining, exactly 10 black cards, all clubs but one — is guaranteed rather than genuinely random. At the end of each round, the previous pile is discarded, narrowing the deck down toward the final, pre-planned punchline: the Ace of Spades. This requires significant practice with the false shuffle and the face-up/face-down mixing sequence before performing it live.

title: Stacked Deck
text:
Step-by-Step Plan

0 (Pre-tasks)

Write down all five hypothesis pairs in advance and seal or hide them (e.g. in envelopes, or on slides revealed one at a time) so the class can confirm you predicted the outcome before seeing the cards
Practice the false shuffle and the face-up/face-down control sequence until it looks convincingly random, see guide below:




1 (Setup)
Hold up the deck and say:

“Before I touch this deck, I’ve already written down five predictions about what will happen as I shuffle and deal these cards. Each prediction has a ‘boring’ expected outcome — the null hypothesis — and a much rarer outcome — the alternative hypothesis. Let’s see which one actually happens each time.”

Shuffle the deck using your false shuffle in full view of the class.


2 (Prediction 1 — Face-up vs Face-down)
Reveal the first sealed prediction. Ask the class:

“If I mix these cards face-up and face-down randomly, would you expect roughly equal numbers of each, or a clear imbalance?”

Deal through the deck, mixing cards face-up and face-down. Count the result. Reveal that face-down cards outnumber face-up cards — matching \(H_1\), not \(H_0\).
Discard the face-up pile, keeping only the face-down cards for the next round.


3 (Prediction 2 — Number Cards Only)
Reveal the second sealed prediction. Ask the class:

“Of the cards we have left, would you expect a mix of number cards and picture cards, or something more unusual?”

Turn over the remaining cards. Reveal that only number cards remain — again matching \(H_1\).
Discard any picture cards (there shouldn’t be any, but this keeps the “elimination” pattern consistent), keeping the number cards for the next round.


4 (Prediction 3 — Exactly 10 Black Cards)
Reveal the third sealed prediction. Ask the class:

“Of these remaining number cards, would you expect a mix of red and black, or something more specific?”

Sort the cards by colour. Reveal exactly 10 black cards — a strikingly specific outcome to have predicted in advance.
Discard the red cards, keeping the 10 black cards for the next round.


5 (Prediction 4 — Clubs Only… Almost)
Reveal the fourth sealed prediction. Ask the class:

“Of these 10 black cards, would you expect a mix of spades and clubs, or only clubs?”

Sort the black cards. This is the twist: the prediction says “clubs only,” but reveal that there are 9 clubs and 1 spade — meaning \(H_0\) (a mix of spades and clubs) is technically what occurred, not the predicted \(H_1\).
Pause here and let the class notice the mismatch. This is a deliberate teaching moment (see the callout below).






Why Prediction 4 is designed to “fail”





This is the one prediction in the sequence that doesn’t match its stated alternative hypothesis — and that’s intentional. It’s a live demonstration that not every hypothesis test rejects the null, and that a predicted alternative can fail to materialise even in a fully controlled setup. Use this moment to ask: if this were a real experiment and not a trick, how would we interpret a result like this? This is a natural segue into discussing Type I and Type II errors, and the fact that failing to reject \(H_0\) doesn’t mean \(H_0\) is true — only that this particular test didn’t provide evidence against it.





6 (Prediction 5 — The Final Card)
Reveal the fifth and final sealed prediction — it contains only one statement: “The black card that isn’t a club is the Ace of Spades.”
Turn over the single spade. Reveal that it is, in fact, the Ace of Spades — landing the final punchline and tying the whole sequence together as one long, fully pre-determined chain of outcomes.

title: Stacked Deck
text:
How Unlikely Is This, Really?
Assuming a genuinely random shuffle and deal, here’s what each stage of the reveal would cost you in probability — and how those probabilities compound.






Worked example (using one plausible run-through)














Step
Event (if truly random)
Probability
Running total




1
Exactly 30 of 52 cards land face-down (rather than an even 26/26 split)
\(\approx 0.060\)
\(\approx 0.060\)


2
All 30 of those face-down cards happen to be number cards (no picture cards at all)
\(\approx 3.1 \times 10^{-6}\)
\(\approx 1.9 \times 10^{-7}\)


3
Exactly 10 of those 30 number cards turn out to be black
\(\approx 2.2 \times 10^{-4}\)
\(\approx 4.1 \times 10^{-11}\)


4
Of those 10 black cards, exactly 9 are clubs and 1 is a spade
\(\approx 5.4 \times 10^{-4}\)

5
That one spade is specifically the Ace of Spades (1 of 10 possible spade ranks)
\(0.1\)
\(\approx 2.2 \times 10^{-15}\)



Overall probability of this exact sequence happening by pure chance: roughly 1 in 450 trillion.



Ask the class: does that number feel believable for something that “just happened” to occur? This is the same reasoning behind a p-value — an outcome this extreme under the null hypothesis (a genuinely random shuffle and deal) is essentially never going to happen on its own, so something else must be going on. In this case: the deck wasn’t random at all.
Note for the instructor: these figures are illustrative, based on one example run. Recalculate steps 1–4 using your own actual observed counts each time you perform it — the shrinking pattern will hold regardless of the exact numbers, since each additional constraint multiplies in another small probability.

title: Stacked Deck
text:
Bonus / Optional:

Can relate this activity to Type I/II errors and the logic of statistical significance
A few extensions to try:

Calculate the true probabilities: For each step, work out the actual probability of the observed outcome occurring by pure chance (e.g. probability of exactly 10 black cards remaining after random dealing), and compare how small these numbers get when compounded across all five predictions.
Discuss p-hacking: Ask what would happen if, instead of 5 predictions, you’d secretly made 50 and only shown the class the 5 that “worked.” This is a great entry point into p-hacking and the multiple comparisons problem.
Type I vs Type II: Use Prediction 4’s “failure” to concretely define a Type II error (failing to detect a real effect) versus a Type I error (falsely detecting an effect that isn’t there).
Discuss trust and evidence: Ask the class how their confidence in your “predictive powers” would change if you’d gotten 4 out of 5 right versus 5 out of 5 — and connect this to how much evidence is “enough” to reject a null hypothesis in real research.

title: Psychopath Test
text: Between-Subjects Design Independent Samples t-Test Group Comparison Psychology

title: Psychopath Test
text:
About
This activity uses a famous (if unproven) riddle to split the class into two independent groups, those who solve it and those who don’t, and compares their scores on a short psychopathy questionnaire. We will treat this as is a genuinely between-subjects design: each student belongs to exactly one group, and the two groups are compared against each other rather than against themselves. It’s a natural setup for the independent samples t-test.

title: Psychopath Test
text: Demonstration

title: Psychopath Test
text:
Materials

Access to a short online psychopathy questionnaire — e.g. Psychology Today’s Psychopathy Test
A tool for students to submit their score and riddle group in real time (e.g. Google Forms)
The riddle text, ready to display on screen (see below)
Paper for students to write their riddle answer independently
A spreadsheet or R session set up to run the independent samples t-test live

title: Psychopath Test
text:
The Riddle
Display this on screen so every student sees it at exactly the same time:

This is a story about a girl.
While at the funeral of her own mother, she met a guy whom she did not know. She thought this guy was amazing, so much the dream guy that she was searching for that she fell in love with him immediately.
However, she never asked for his name or number and afterward could not find anyone who knew who he was.
A few days later the girl killed her own sister.
Question: Why did she kill her sister?







Answer (for the instructor only — don’t reveal until after data collection)





She reasoned that if the guy appeared at her mother’s funeral, he might appear at another family funeral too — so she killed her sister in the hope of seeing him again.
Note for the class: there’s a persistent (but never actually proven) claim that this riddle was used by an American psychologist to test for psychopathic thinking, and that several apprehended serial killers answered it correctly. Treat this as an interesting hook rather than a verified fact — it’s worth being upfront with students that this origin story is folklore rather than documented research, which is itself a nice discussion point about how “psychology facts” spread.

title: Psychopath Test
text:
Step-by-Step Plan

0 (Pre-tasks)

Test the psychopathy questionnaire link yourself and confirm it produces a clear numeric score
Set up a submission form with three fields: (1) Name/ID, (2) psychopathy score, (3) whether they solved the riddle correctly (Yes/No)
Prepare the riddle slide, ready to display but not yet shown



1 (Setup)
Explain the two-part process to the class without revealing the riddle yet:

“In a moment, I’m going to show you a short riddle. I want everyone to try to solve it silently and write your answer down on paper — don’t say it out loud, don’t discuss it with your neighbour. This needs to stay independent, so please keep your answer to yourself for now.”



2 (Present the Riddle)
Display the riddle on screen for the whole class simultaneously. Give students a fixed amount of time (e.g. 2–3 minutes) to write their answer down on paper.


3 (Reveal and Group)
Reveal the correct answer. Have students self-report (via the form) whether their written answer matched — this sorts the class into two groups:

Group 1: Solved the riddle correctly
Group 2: Did not solve the riddle correctly



4 (Complete the Psychopathy Questionnaire)
Direct students to complete the psychopathy questionnaire and record their score through the form, alongside their riddle group from Step 3.


5 (Set Up the Hypotheses)
Before running the test, formalise what’s being compared:
\[
H_0: \mu_{\text{solved}} = \mu_{\text{not solved}}
\]
\[
H_1: \mu_{\text{solved}} \neq \mu_{\text{not solved}}
\]
where \(\mu_{\text{solved}}\) and \(\mu_{\text{not solved}}\) are the true mean psychopathy scores for each group.


6 (Explore the Data)
Before calculating anything, look at the two groups’ distributions side by side (e.g. boxplots or a simple dot plot of scores by group). Ask the class:

“Just from looking at this, does it look like the two groups differ much? What would make you confident either way?”



7 (Run the Independent Samples t-Test)
Calculate the test statistic comparing the two independent groups.






Formula: Independent Samples t-Test





\[
t = \frac{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2}{\sqrt{\dfrac{s_1^2}{n_1} + \dfrac{s_2^2}{n_2}}}
\]
where:

\(\bar{x}_1, \bar{x}_2\) = mean psychopathy score for each group
\(s_1^2, s_2^2\) = variance of scores within each group
\(n_1, n_2\) = number of students in each group

Degrees of freedom (using the Welch–Satterthwaite approximation, which doesn’t assume equal variances):
\[
df \approx \frac{\left(\dfrac{s_1^2}{n_1} + \dfrac{s_2^2}{n_2}\right)^2}{\dfrac{(s_1^2/n_1)^2}{n_1 - 1} + \dfrac{(s_2^2/n_2)^2}{n_2 - 1}}
\]



Compare the calculated \(t\) to the critical value (or compute the exact p-value) and decide whether to reject \(H_0\).


8 (Discuss)
Work through these questions as a class:

Why is this a between-subjects design rather than a within-subjects one? What would a within-subjects version of this study even look like (and would it make sense here)?
If a significant difference is found, does that mean solving the riddle causes higher psychopathy scores? What alternative explanations exist (e.g. general problem-solving ability, prior exposure to the riddle, self-selection in who answers honestly)?
What might explain groups being very unequal in size (e.g. only 3 students solve it, 40 don’t)? How does that unevenness affect how much you’d trust the result?
Given the shaky, unverified origin story behind this riddle, how should that affect how much weight we put on the result even if it is statistically significant?

title: Psychopath Test
text:
Bonus / Optional:

Can relate this activity to effect size and unequal sample sizes
A few extensions to try:

Effect size: Calculate Cohen’s \(d\) for the group difference, to discuss how large the gap is, not just whether it’s statistically detectable.
Equal variance assumption: Compare the standard Student’s t-test (equal variances assumed) to Welch’s t-test (unequal variances allowed) and discuss when each is appropriate — this is a good moment to introduce Levene’s test for equality of variances.
Non-parametric alternative: If the psychopathy scores look skewed rather than normally distributed, introduce the Mann-Whitney U test as a non-parametric alternative to the independent samples t-test.
Replicate the folklore: Search for the actual origin of this riddle claim as a class exercise in evaluating psychological “urban legends” — a nice tie-in to research literacy and misinformation about psychology.

title: Movie Posters
text: Inter-Rater Reliability Cohen’s Kappa Agreement Categorical Data

title: Movie Posters
text:
About
This activity uses movie posters to introduce inter-rater reliability, a core concept whenever multiple people (raters, judges, coders) are asked to classify the same thing and you need to know how much their judgments actually agree. Students are shown a series of obscure, mostly unknown movie posters with the title blacked out, and simply guess the genre from the visual alone. Because nobody actually knows the “correct” answer, this isn’t really about accuracy — it’s about how consistently different people converge on the same interpretation, which is exactly the question Cohen’s Kappa is built to answer.

title: Movie Posters
text: Demonstration

title: Movie Posters
text:
Materials

10 movie posters from fairly obscure/arthouse films (title and any obvious genre text blacked out or cropped out). Below are some samples:

A tool for students to submit their genre guess per poster (e.g. Google Forms)
A fixed, shared list of genre categories for students to choose from (e.g. Horror, Comedy, Drama, Thriller, Romance, Sci-Fi)
A spreadsheet or R session set up to calculate agreement statistics live

title: Movie Posters
text:
Step-by-Step Plan

0 (Pre-tasks)

Select 10 movie posters, ideally from lesser-known or foreign/arthouse films — the less recognisable the film, the more the guesses reflect genuine visual interpretation rather than prior knowledge
Edit each poster to remove the title, tagline, and any text that gives away the genre directly (e.g. “A Hilarious New Comedy”)
Decide on a fixed set of genre categories in advance, so every student is choosing from the same options (open-ended text responses are much harder to score for agreement)
Set up the submission form with one question per poster, using the same category list each time



1 (Setup)
Display the first poster and explain the task:

“I’m going to show you 10 movie posters, one at a time. The titles have been removed. I just want you to guess the genre, based purely on what you see. There’s no ‘correct’ answer I’m expecting — I’m actually more interested in whether you all agree with each other than whether you’re right. Note: some movies can have multiple genres, just pick what you think is the main one.”



2 (Collect Judgments)
Show each poster for a fixed amount of time (e.g. 15–20 seconds), and have students submit their genre guess before moving to the next one. Repeat for all 10 posters.


3 (Reveal the Films)
Once all judgments are collected, reveal the actual title and genre of each film. Let the class react to how close (or far off) their guesses were, but keep the focus on the next step — this reveal is mostly for fun/context, not the main statistical point.


4 (Explore Agreement — Two Raters)
Pick any two students at random and compare their 10 genre guesses side by side.






Simple (Naive) Percent Agreement





\[
P_o = \frac{\text{Number of posters both raters agreed on}}{\text{Total number of posters}}
\]
This is the most intuitive way to measure agreement, but it has a major flaw: two raters could agree by pure chance, especially if one genre (e.g. “Drama”) is a common guess. Percent agreement doesn’t account for this.





5 (Introduce Cohen’s Kappa)
Cohen’s Kappa corrects for the agreement we’d expect by chance alone, giving a more honest measure of how much two raters actually agree beyond guessing.






Formula: Cohen’s Kappa





\[
\kappa = \frac{P_o - P_e}{1 - P_e}
\]
where:

\(P_o\) = observed proportion of agreement (from Step 4)
\(P_e\) = expected proportion of agreement by chance, calculated from the marginal proportions of each genre each rater used

\[
P_e = \sum_{i} p_{A_i} \cdot p_{B_i}
\]
where \(p_{A_i}\) and \(p_{B_i}\) are the proportion of times Rater A and Rater B each chose genre \(i\).



Walk through the calculation live using your two selected students’ data, building the confusion matrix (a genre-by-genre table of who guessed what) on the board first, since \(P_e\) depends on it directly.


6 (Interpret Kappa)
Discuss what the resulting \(\kappa\) value actually means:



Kappa Range
Interpretation




< 0
Worse than chance agreement


0.01 – 0.20
Slight agreement


0.21 – 0.40
Fair agreement


0.41 – 0.60
Moderate agreement


0.61 – 0.80
Substantial agreement


0.81 – 1.00
Almost perfect agreement



Ask the class: does the calculated \(\kappa\) feel surprising, given how confident individual students may have felt about their own guesses?


7 (Scale Up — Whole Class Agreement)
Two raters is a nice starting point, but the real dataset involves the whole class. Introduce Fleiss’ Kappa as the extension of Cohen’s Kappa to more than two raters, and calculate it for the full class’s judgments on all 10 posters.






Formula: Fleiss’ Kappa (concept)





\[
\kappa = \frac{\bar{P} - \bar{P_e}}{1 - \bar{P_e}}
\]
where \(\bar{P}\) is the mean observed agreement across all posters and raters, and \(\bar{P_e}\) is the mean expected agreement by chance, calculated from how often each genre was chosen overall across the whole class.



Discuss how this whole-class \(\kappa\) compares to the two-student value calculated earlier — is agreement higher or lower once everyone is included?

title: Movie Posters
text:
Bonus / Optional:

Can relate this activity to real-world applications of inter-rater reliability
A few extensions to try:

Poster-by-poster breakdown: Calculate agreement separately for each of the 10 posters — which posters had the highest agreement, and which were the most contested? Discuss what visual features might drive consensus versus disagreement.
Real-world context: Discuss where inter-rater reliability actually matters in practice — e.g. medical diagnoses from imaging, essay grading, content moderation, or coding qualitative interview data — and why researchers report kappa values in these settings.
Chance agreement demo: Show what happens to \(\kappa\) if two “raters” guessed completely randomly (simulate this) — it should hover near 0, even though raw percent agreement might still look moderately high by chance alone.
Weighted kappa: For genres that are “closer” to each other (e.g. Thriller vs. Horror) versus totally different (e.g. Comedy vs. Horror), introduce weighted kappa, which penalises near-miss disagreements less than totally opposite ones.

title: Loaded Dices
text: Central Limit Theorem Simulation Discrete Probability Sampling Distributions

title: Loaded Dices
text:
About
This is an instructor-led demonstration of the Central Limit Theorem using two secretly loaded dice. Before any rolling happens, the instructor seals an envelope with a precise prediction about where the running total of many rolls will land. Because the dice are rigged, this “impossible” prediction is guaranteed — but the deeper lesson is that the same shape (a bell curve) would emerge from summing enough rolls even with fair dice. The bias is what makes the trick land; the Central Limit Theorem is what makes it true either way.






Note



Students may get bored if you are performing 40-50 rolls yourself. Either reduce this number or acquire more loaded dices, so that you can invite some students up to do this simultaneously. With 5 sets of loaded (i.e. 10 dices), you can get ask each student to roll 5 times relatively quickly.

title: Loaded Dices
text: Demonstration

title: Loaded Dices
text:
Materials

Two dice with a known, deliberate bias — e.g. weighted dice, dice with rounded edges, or novelty/magic-shop dice designed to favour certain faces (see Pre-tasks)
A regular fair die or two, for later comparison
A sealed envelope or hidden slide for your prediction
A document camera or projector so the class can see each roll clearly
A whiteboard, spreadsheet, or slide to build the running histogram live in front of the class

title: Loaded Dices
text:
Step-by-Step Plan

0 (Pre-tasks)

Obtain two loaded dice and determine each one’s true long-run average roll value in advance — either from the manufacturer’s spec, or by rolling each several hundred times yourself beforehand and recording the empirical mean and standard deviation
Calculate the combined mean and variance of rolling both dice together and summing them: \(\mu = \mu_A + \mu_B\), \(\sigma^2 = \sigma_A^2 + \sigma_B^2\)
Decide on a fixed number of rolls you’ll perform in class (e.g. 40–50 rolls of both dice together)
Using the CLT formula (see Step 4), calculate the expected range for the running total’s distribution after all rolls, and write your prediction in the sealed envelope
Make sure the loaded dice are visually indistinguishable from fair dice — the class shouldn’t be able to tell just by looking at them



1 (Setup)
Hold up the two dice and the sealed envelope. Say:

“I’m going to roll these two dice together, over and over, and add up the total each time. Before I roll a single die, I’ve already sealed a prediction in this envelope about the shape and location of the results we’re about to see. Let’s find out if I’m right.”



2 (Roll and Record)
Roll both dice together under the document camera, sum the two faces, and record the result on the board or a live spreadsheet. Repeat this for your predetermined number of rolls (e.g. 40–50 times), narrating occasionally:

“Watch — each roll on its own just gives us a number between 2 and 12. Nothing special about any single roll.”



3 (Build the Histogram)
As results accumulate, plot a running histogram of all the roll-sums so far, updating it live after each roll (or in small batches, e.g. every 5 rolls, if that’s easier to manage). Ask the class:

“We’re just adding two numbers each time. Would you expect the pile of totals to end up random and shapeless, or to settle into some kind of pattern?”

Let the histogram build in front of them — it should settle into a smooth, roughly symmetric, bell-like shape, centred somewhere other than where a fair pair of dice would center.


4 (The Reveal)
Open the envelope. Reveal your prediction, and show that the actual accumulated results land almost exactly where you said they would — both in shape and in location.






How the trick works





Both dice were secretly loaded with a known bias, so their true combined mean, \(\mu\), isn’t 7 like a fair pair of dice, and their combined variance, \(\sigma^2\), isn’t the standard value either. Because you measured each die’s true parameters in advance (Step 0), you could predict exactly where the running total’s distribution would settle using the Central Limit Theorem:
\[
\text{Sum of } n \text{ rolls} \sim \text{Approximately } N\left(n\mu,\; n\sigma^2\right)
\]
For \(n\) rolls, the predicted range for the running total was:
\[
n\mu \pm 2\sqrt{n\sigma^2}
\]
This is what let you write a precise, narrow prediction in advance — not psychic ability, just knowing the true (biased) parameters of the dice before the class did.





5 (Compare to Fair Dice)
Now repeat the same process using two genuinely fair dice — either live, if time allows, or using a pre-built simulation you can display instantly (recommended, to save class time). Build a second histogram alongside the first.
Ask the class:

“Both histograms look roughly bell-shaped. What’s actually different between them?”

Guide them to notice: the shape (approximately normal) is similar in both cases, but the loaded dice’s histogram is shifted away from where fair dice would centre (7). This is the key insight — the Central Limit Theorem guarantees the shape, not the location. Any pair of dice, fair or loaded, produces a roughly normal distribution of sums as the number of rolls grows; only the true mean and variance of the dice determine where that bell curve sits.

title: Loaded Dices
text:
Bonus / Optional:

Can relate this activity to sample size and the shrinking of standard error
A few extensions to try:

Vary the roll count: Show pre-simulated histograms built from 10, 50, and 500 rolls, and compare how much “smoother” and narrower the resulting distribution becomes as the roll count increases.
Detecting the load: Ask the class how many rolls it would take before they could statistically detect the dice were loaded, just from the shift in the histogram — a nice callback to the hypothesis-testing and card-trick activities.
Single die vs. summed pair: Show a histogram of individual die faces (1–6, roughly flat/biased but not bell-shaped) next to the summed-pair histogram (bell-shaped). This reinforces that CLT applies to sums/averages, not raw individual outcomes.
Simulate instead of roll: If class time is short, simulate thousands of virtual rolls of both fair and loaded dice pairs (e.g. in R) and overlay the resulting histograms, letting students see the CLT effect at a much larger sample size than is feasible by hand.

title: Heart Rates
text: Within-Subjects Design Paired Design Repeated Measures ANOVA Physiological Data

title: Heart Rates
text:
About
This activity turns the whole class into their own control group. Each student measures their own resting heart rate as a baseline, then watches three short video clips designed to trigger different emotional states: fear, sadness, and arousal, recording their heart rate after each one. Because every student contributes a baseline and three follow-up measurements, this is a live, hands-on introduction to within-subjects (repeated measures) design, where each participant acts as their own control, removing a lot of the between-person variability that a between-subjects design would have to deal with.

title: Heart Rates
text: Demonstration

title: Heart Rates
text:
Materials

A visible countdown timer (60s, or 30s if you want a quicker task — see Step 2)
3 short (~1 minute) video clips, one each for fear, sadness, and arousal (see Pre-tasks)
A way to dim/turn off the lecture hall lights, for added atmosphere during the fear and sadness clips
A tool for students to record their heart rate readings after each stage (e.g. Google Forms, or a simple show-of-hands/paper tally if you’d rather keep it low-tech)
Optional: a pre-prepared dataset from a previous run of this activity, for the within-subjects ANOVA walkthrough in Step 6

title: Heart Rates
text:
Step-by-Step Plan

0 (Pre-tasks)

Select a ~1 minute fear clip (plenty available on YouTube — jump-scare compilations or horror clip snippets work well)
Select a ~1 minute sad clip (a well-known emotional film scene works well here)
Decide how you’ll handle the “arousal” stimulus — see the note in Step 5
Set up your countdown timer and data collection form in advance
If using a pre-prepared dataset for Step 6, have it ready to load and analyse live



1 (Setup)
Explain the activity to the class:

“Today you’re the data. We’re going to measure your heart rate at rest, and then again after three short video clips designed to trigger different emotions. Everyone will have a baseline measurement and three follow-up measurements — so each of you is essentially your own control group.”

Show students how to find their pulse — usually at the wrist (radial artery, on the thumb side) or the neck (carotid artery, just beside the windpipe).





2 (Baseline Heart Rate)
Have students sit quietly and locate their pulse. Start the 60-second countdown timer on screen and say “start.” When the timer hits zero, say “stop.”

If you’re short on time, a 30-second count multiplied by 2 works almost as well for a classroom demonstration — it doesn’t need to be clinically precise, just a consistent baseline.

Have students record their baseline heart rate (beats per minute).


3 (Stimulus 1 — Fear)
Dim or turn off the lights for effect. Play the fear clip.
Immediately afterward, have students find their pulse again and re-time (60s or 30s x2, matching whatever method you used for the baseline). Record heart rate as “Fear.”


4 (Stimulus 2 — Sadness)
Play the sad clip (lights can stay dimmed for continued effect).
Repeat the same heart rate measurement process. Record heart rate as “Sadness.”


5 (Stimulus 3 — Arousal)
For the arousal condition, say something like:

“I have to keep this class PG-rated, so for this one, just close your eyes and imagine whatever you’d like for the next minute.”

This usually gets a laugh and works surprisingly well as a stand-in stimulus without needing any actual video content.
Repeat the heart rate measurement process. Record heart rate as “Arousal.”


6 (Analyse as a Class)
Compile the four measurements per student (Baseline, Fear, Sadness, Arousal) into a single dataset — either using the class’s live data or a pre-prepared dataset from a previous run, if you’d rather not wait on data entry.






Why this is a within-subjects design





Because every student contributes a measurement under all four conditions, each student acts as their own control. This removes between-person variability (e.g. some people naturally have higher resting heart rates than others) from the comparison, making it much easier to detect whether the stimuli themselves caused a change — a key advantage of paired/within-subjects designs over between-subjects designs.



Start with the simplest comparison — baseline vs. one stimulus — using a paired t-test:
\[
t = \frac{\bar{d}}{s_d / \sqrt{n}}
\]
where:

\(\bar{d}\) = mean of the differences (stimulus heart rate − baseline heart rate) across students
\(s_d\) = standard deviation of those differences
\(n\) = number of students

Then extend to comparing all three stimuli at once using repeated measures ANOVA:
\[
F = \frac{MS_{\text{condition}}}{MS_{\text{error}}}
\]
where \(MS_{\text{condition}}\) captures variability between the fear/sadness/arousal conditions, and \(MS_{\text{error}}\) captures the leftover within-subject variability once each student’s own baseline tendency has been accounted for.


7 (Discuss)
Ask the class:

Which condition produced the biggest average increase from baseline? Does that match what you’d expect physiologically?
Was the change consistent across students, or did some people barely react while others spiked?
Why might a between-subjects version of this experiment (different groups of students each watching only one clip) be a noisier, less reliable design than what we just did?

title: Heart Rates
text:
Bonus / Optional:

Can relate this activity to effect size and individual variability
A few extensions to try:

Order effects: Discuss what might happen if every class always watched fear → sadness → arousal in the same order — could earlier stimuli “carry over” and affect later readings? Introduce the idea of counterbalancing as a solution.
Effect size: Beyond just significance, calculate Cohen’s \(d\) for one of the paired comparisons to discuss how large the heart rate change was, not just whether it was statistically detectable.
Individual differences: Plot each student’s four measurements as a connected line (a “spaghetti plot”) to show how much the pattern of response varies person to person, even when the average trend is consistent.
Post-hoc comparisons: If the repeated measures ANOVA is significant, discuss why you can’t just conclude “the conditions differ” — introduce pairwise post-hoc tests (e.g. Bonferroni-corrected paired t-tests) to identify which specific conditions differ from each other.

title: Find Your Cluster
text: K-Means Clustering Unsupervised Learning Multivariate Data Standardisation

title: Find Your Cluster
text:
About
This activity uses a short self-report app to give every student a personal profile across six dimensions: Speed, Risk, Structure, Ambiguity, Social, and Pattern — covering things like how quickly they make decisions, how comfortable they are with uncertainty, and whether they lean toward independent or collaborative work. Once the whole class has a six-number profile, the instructor runs k-means clustering live to sort students into groups based on similarity — and if the room allows, students physically move to sit with their cluster, turning an abstract clustering output into something they can immediately feel and discuss.

title: Find Your Cluster
text: Demonstration

title: Find Your Cluster
text:
Materials

The Six Micro-Tests Score App (download below) — each student needs a device to access it




 Six dimensions test





A tool for students to submit their six scores (e.g. Google Forms, or directly via the app’s “Copy CSV” button if you’re collecting responses manually)
A stats package (R recommended) set up to run k-means clustering live
Optional: enough open floor space or movable tables for students to physically regroup by cluster afterward

title: Find Your Cluster
text:
The Six Dimensions



Dimension
What it measures




Speed
Quick vs. careful decision-making


Risk
Cautious vs. risk-seeking responses


Structure
Preference for clear instructions and rules


Ambiguity
Comfort with unclear situations


Social
Independent vs. collaborative working style


Pattern
Rule-based vs. intuitive thinking



Each test has 5 items on a 1–5 scale (with reverse-scored items handled automatically), giving a raw score from 5–25 per dimension, or a mean item score from 1–5.

title: Find Your Cluster
text:
Step-by-Step Plan

0 (Pre-tasks)

Test the app yourself and confirm the “Copy CSV” function works as expected on your setup
Set up a submission form (or a shared spreadsheet) where students can paste in their name and six scores
Have your R session or spreadsheet ready with a k-means script prepared in advance (see Step 4), so you’re not writing code live in front of the class



1 (Setup)
Direct students to the app and explain the task:

“You’re going to complete six very short tests, each with 5 quick questions. Just answer honestly and quickly — there’s no right or wrong answer here. Give yourself 5 to 10 minutes to get through all six.”



2 (Complete the Tests)
Give students 5–10 minutes to work through all six tests in the app. Once finished, they click “Calculate scores” and then “Copy CSV” to get their six-dimension profile.


3 (Collect the Data)
Have students paste their name and six scores into your shared submission form or spreadsheet. Compile the full class dataset — each row is one student, each column is one of the six dimension scores.


4 (Standardise the Data)
Before running k-means, standardise each dimension so no single test dominates the clustering just because it happens to have more spread.






Why standardise first?





K-means clustering is based on distance between points. If one dimension has a much larger range or variance than the others, it will dominate the distance calculation and effectively drown out the other five dimensions. Standardising each column to a mean of 0 and standard deviation of 1 puts all six dimensions on equal footing.
\[
z = \frac{x - \bar{x}}{s}
\]



scores_raw <- read.csv("class_scores.csv")
scores_z <- scale(scores_raw[, c("speed","risk","structure","ambiguity","social","pattern")])


5 (Choose the Number of Clusters)
Before running k-means, decide how many clusters (\(k\)) to use. A simple, visual approach for class purposes is the elbow method: plot total within-cluster variation against different values of \(k\), and look for the point where adding more clusters stops giving a big improvement.
wss <- sapply(1:8, function(k) kmeans(scores_z, centers = k, nstart = 10)$tot.withinss)
plot(1:8, wss, type = "b", xlab = "Number of clusters (k)", ylab = "Within-cluster sum of squares")
Discuss with the class where the “elbow” appears to be, and pick a \(k\) that’s small enough to be meaningful for regrouping the room (e.g. 3–5 clusters).


6 (Run K-Means)
set.seed(123)
km <- kmeans(scores_z, centers = 4, nstart = 25)
scores_raw$cluster <- km$cluster
Display each student’s assigned cluster alongside their name.


7 (Interpret the Clusters)
For each cluster, calculate the average (standardised) score on each of the six dimensions, and display it as a table or radar-style summary.
aggregate(scores_z, by = list(cluster = km$cluster), FUN = mean)
Ask the class to help name each cluster based on its profile — e.g. a cluster high on Risk and low on Structure might get nicknamed “The Improvisers,” while a cluster high on Structure and Pattern might be “The Planners.”


8 (Move and Discuss)
If the room allows, announce each student’s cluster and have them physically move to sit with their group.
Once seated together, give each group a few minutes to discuss:

Do you feel like this cluster actually describes you? Why or why not?
What do you have in common with the others at your table, beyond just the six numbers?
Is there a dimension where your group is surprisingly split, even though you were clustered together overall?

title: Find Your Cluster
text:
Bonus / Optional:

Can relate this activity to dimensionality and the curse of high dimensions
A few extensions to try:

Visualise in 2D: Run PCA on the standardised data and plot the first two principal components, coloured by cluster, so students can see a 2D “map” of the whole class.
Compare k values: Re-run the clustering with a different \(k\) (e.g. 3 vs. 6) and discuss how the groupings — and the physical seating — would have changed.
Hierarchical clustering: Run an agglomerative hierarchical clustering on the same data and display a dendrogram, comparing which students get grouped together versus the k-means result.
Stability check: Re-run k-means a few times with different random starting points (nstart) and discuss why the algorithm can converge to different results depending on initialisation — a nice segue into why nstart with multiple restarts is standard practice.

title: Four Aces
text: Probability Sampling Without Replacement Conditional Probability Multiplication Rule

title: Four Aces
text:
About
This activity uses a simple card trick to build intuition for probability without replacement — one of the trickiest ideas for students to grasp because each draw changes the probabilities for the next one. Students predict the probability of drawing an ace at each step, watch the instructor “defy the odds” by pulling an ace every time, and then unpack why the trick works using the multiplication rule for dependent events.

title: Four Aces
text: Demonstration

title: Four Aces
text:
Materials

A standard deck of 52 playing cards (with all 4 aces easily locatable — see Pre-tasks)
A whiteboard or slide to record probabilities as you go
A table or document camera so the class can see the deck (optional, but adds drama)

title: Four Aces
text:
Step-by-Step Plan

0 (Pre-tasks)

Before class, arrange the deck so all 4 aces are on top of the deck (this is your setup for the trick — see the callout in Step 2)
Practice a false shuffle: a shuffle that looks random to the audience but keeps the top few cards (your aces) in place. Here is one example of a false shuffle, where you involve two spectators to both say “stop” at any time fo their choosing:




1 (Setup)
Hold up the deck (shuffled with your false shuffle, aces secretly on top) and say:

“This is a standard, well-shuffled deck of 52 cards. I’m going to draw cards one at a time, and each time, I want you to tell me: what’s the probability that the card I draw is an ace?”



2 (First Draw)
Ask the class:

“What’s the probability that the first card I draw is an ace?”

Write the answer on the board:
\[
P(\text{Ace}_1) = \frac{4}{52}
\]






How the trick works





Because the deck is secretly stacked with all 4 aces on top (and your shuffle only ever moved cards below them), the top card is guaranteed to be an ace no matter what the class thinks the odds are. Draw the top card with normal, unhurried motion — don’t rush this draw, since the “reveal” only works if it looks like a genuine, random draw from a full deck.



Reveal the card. It’s an ace. Let the class react.


3 (Second Draw — Without Replacement)
Set the ace aside (do not return it to the deck — this is the “without replacement” part) and ask:

“Now that one ace is gone and the deck has one fewer card, what’s the probability the next card I draw is also an ace?”

Guide the class to the updated probability:
\[
P(\text{Ace}_2 \mid \text{Ace}_1) = \frac{3}{51}
\]
Draw the second card from the top (again, secretly still an ace) and reveal it.


4 (Third and Fourth Draws)
Repeat the process, updating the probability each time and writing the running multiplication on the board:
\[
P(\text{Ace}_3 \mid \text{Ace}_1, \text{Ace}_2) = \frac{2}{50}
\]
\[
P(\text{Ace}_4 \mid \text{Ace}_1, \text{Ace}_2, \text{Ace}_3) = \frac{1}{49}
\]
By the fourth draw, students should notice the probability is shrinking fast — and yet you pull the ace again.


5 (Reveal the Full Picture)
Once all 4 aces are on the table, ask the class:

“What’s the probability that all four of my draws were aces, if I were really just drawing randomly from a full deck each time?”

Build up the joint probability using the multiplication rule for dependent events:
\[
P(\text{all 4 aces}) = \frac{4}{52} \times \frac{3}{51} \times \frac{2}{50} \times \frac{1}{49} \approx 0.0000037
\]
Let that number sink in — roughly a 1-in-270,725 chance. Then reveal the trick: the deck was stacked in advance, and this is exactly why the result felt “too good to be true.” Tie it back to the earlier card activity: an outcome this improbable under random drawing is strong evidence that the process wasn’t actually random — the same logic as a hypothesis test.

title: Four Aces
text:
Bonus / Optional:

Can relate this activity to combinatorics and hypergeometric distributions
A few extensions to try:

Compare with replacement: Ask what the probability would have been with replacement (returning each card and reshuffling before the next draw) — \(\left(\frac{4}{52}\right)^4\) — and discuss why it’s different (and much smaller) than the without-replacement version.
Generalise the formula: Introduce the hypergeometric distribution as the general tool for “probability of k successes when sampling without replacement,” and connect it back to this specific case.
Flip the trick: Ask students to calculate the probability of drawing 4 aces in a row if you hadn’t stacked the deck — this is the number you just calculated — and discuss what threshold of “surprising” would make them suspect a stacked deck in real life.
Different depths: What if you only wanted to guarantee the first 2 draws are aces, not all 4? How does the stacking strategy — and the multiplication — change?

title: Want to Contribute?

I believe teaching is, at its core, about collaboration. The best classroom activities are rarely invented in isolation. They’re passed between colleagues, tweaked in a tutorial, refined after a lecture that didn’t quite land, and shared over a coffee break. Some of the hooks on this site started life exactly that way, borrowed and adapted from other educators generous enough to share what worked (and what did not) for them.
That’s the spirit behind making this resource open access. Good teaching materials shouldn’t sit locked away in one person’s slide deck, only ever used once a year by one class. The hope is that by putting these hooks out in the open, other educators can pick them up, adapt them to their own courses, and hopefully build on them further, the same way I’ve built on ideas from others.
If you have an activity, demonstration, or story you think would work well here, I’d love to hear about it. Chances are you’ve got a hook of your own that consistently gets a room’s attention, and this collection only gets better the more perspectives it draws on.
