title: Heads Every Time
text: Binomial Distribution Probability Independent Trials Expected Value

title: Heads Every Time
text:
About
This activity uses a coin-flipping trick as a hook into the binomial distribution. Students first calculate the probability of an instructor “getting lucky” with heads a few times in a row, and are suitably unimpressed when it happens once or twice. But as the run of heads keeps going, the class starts to realise the odds of pure chance are shrinking fast, setting up a discussion of the binomial distribution, independent trials, and how we decide when a result is too surprising to be random.

title: Heads Every Time
text: Demonstration

title: Heads Every Time
text:
Materials

A coin (a slightly weighted or grippy coin can make the technique in Step 0 easier, but a standard coin works fine with practice)
A whiteboard or slide to record probabilities as you go
A table or document camera so the class can see each flip clearly

title: Heads Every Time
text:
Step-by-Step Plan

0 (Pre-tasks)
Before class, practice the coin-control technique below until it looks like a natural, casual flip, the trick relies on it not looking rehearsed.

The technique relies on a controlled flip rather than a true toss. With practice, the coin can be made to land on the same face almost every time while still looking like a normal flip to onlookers.


1 (Setup)
Hold up the coin and say:

“I’m going to flip this coin several times in a row. Before each flip, I want you to tell me: what’s the probability that it lands heads?”



2 (First Flip)
Ask the class:

“What’s the probability this coin lands heads?”

Write the answer on the board:
\[
P(\text{Heads}) = \frac{1}{2} = 0.5
\]
Flip the coin using your practiced technique. It lands heads. Let the class shrug it off — one heads is nothing special.


3 (Repeated Flips)
Flip again, and again, each time asking the class to update the cumulative probability of seeing this many heads in a row, assuming a fair coin:
\[
P(\text{2 heads in a row}) = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^2 = \frac{1}{4}
\]
\[
P(\text{3 heads in a row}) = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^3 = \frac{1}{8}
\]
\[
P(\text{4 heads in a row}) = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^4 = \frac{1}{16}
\]
Keep going for 6–8 flips, writing the shrinking probability on the board each time. By flip 6 or 7, the class should be visibly suspicious.


4 (The Reveal)
Ask the class:

“If this were really a fair coin, what’s the probability of seeing 8 heads in a row?”

\[
P(\text{8 heads in a row}) = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^8 = \frac{1}{256} \approx 0.0039
\]
Reveal the technique from Step 0. Tie it back to the earlier activities: a result this improbable under a “fair” process is exactly the kind of evidence that should make us question whether the process really was fair — the same logic used in the card trick and cup-tasting demonstrations.


5 (Formalise the Binomial Distribution)
Introduce the general binomial formula, using the coin flips as a running example:
\[
P(X = k) = \binom{n}{k} p^k (1-p)^{n-k}
\]
where:

\(n\) = number of flips
\(k\) = number of heads
\(p\) = probability of heads on a single flip (0.5 for a fair coin)

Work through an example as a class: what’s the probability of getting exactly 5 heads out of 8 flips (not necessarily in a row) with a fair coin?
\[
P(X = 5) = \binom{8}{5} (0.5)^5 (0.5)^3 = 56 \times 0.03125 \times 0.125 \approx 0.219
\]
Contrast this with the probability of 8 heads in a row, calculated earlier — this is a good moment to highlight the difference between “exactly k successes in any order” versus “k successes in a specific sequence.”

title: Heads Every Time
text:
Bonus / Optional:

Can relate this activity to expected value and variance
A few extensions to try:

Expected value: Ask how many heads students would expect out of 8 fair flips on average, introducing \(E(X) = np\).
Live simulation: Have the whole class flip real coins simultaneously (8 flips each) and tally how many people got runs of 5+ heads in a row, comparing the empirical rate to the theoretical \(1/32\) probability.
Vary p: Discuss how the binomial formula changes for a biased coin (e.g. \(p = 0.7\)), and how much more likely a run of heads becomes.
Link to hypothesis testing: Introduce the idea of a significance threshold — at what point (5 heads? 6? 8?) would the class have been justified in calling out “that’s not a fair coin” before the reveal?

title: Bad Graphs Gallery
text: Data Visualisation Misleading Graphs Critical thinking

title: Bad Graphs Gallery
text:
About
This activity turns students into data detectives. By examining real graphs that have been published in the news, on social media, or in official reports, students learn to spot the tricks — truncated axes, misleading scales, cherry-picked data, poor chart choices — that can distort how a graph is interpreted. The activity builds critical data literacy skills while reinforcing what makes a graph good by contrast.

title: Bad Graphs Gallery
text: Demonstration

title: Bad Graphs Gallery
text:
Materials

A collection of real “bad graph” examples (screenshots or links) sourced from news articles, social media, or reports
A tool for students to respond in real time or in small groups (e.g. Google Forms, Padlet, or simple discussion)

Here are some that I have found (mostly from Fox News)

OriginalRevisions














OriginalRevisions














OriginalRevisions














OriginalRevisions














OriginalRevisions














OriginalRevisions







This one here looks like people were allowed to choose multiple options (I think that’s why it exceeds 100%). Choose a different type of graph.

title: Bad Graphs Gallery
text:
Step-by-Step Plan

0 (Pre-tasks)

Curate 4–6 examples of poorly constructed or misleading graphs (truncated y-axis, dual axes, 3D pie charts, cherry-picked timeframes, etc.)
For each graph, prepare the correct or redrawn version if possible, to reveal later
Optionally set up a short form or worksheet with prompts like “What is this graph trying to tell you?” and “What’s actually misleading about it?”



1 (Setup)
In class (face-to-face or online), display the first graph and say:

“This graph was published in [source]. Take 30 seconds — what’s your first impression? What story does it seem to tell?”



2 (Collect responses)
Have students jot down or submit their first impression of each graph before any discussion — this captures the “gut reaction” the graph was designed to produce.


3 (Diagnose the problem)
Work through each graph as a class or in small groups, identifying the specific technique used to mislead (e.g. truncated axis exaggerating a trend, inconsistent bin widths, area encoding that distorts proportions). Introduce the relevant vocabulary as it comes up.


4 (Redraw / Fix)
Show a corrected version of the graph (or challenge students to sketch one) using the same data. Discuss how the story changes once the distortion is removed.


5 (Reveal)
Reveal the source and context of the original graph, including any explanation from the publisher (if available) or the pushback it received online. Discuss why these distortions are so common — intentional persuasion vs. simple carelessness.

title: Bad Graphs Gallery
text:
Bonus / Optional:

Can relate this activity to critical evaluation of data reporting more broadly
After working through the curated set, try a few extensions:

Student-sourced examples: Ask students to find and submit their own “bad graph” from the past week — from news, social media, or advertising — for the next class.
Redesign challenge: Give students the raw data behind one bad graph and have them redesign the chart from scratch, following good visualisation principles.
Rank the offenders: Have students rank the examples from “misleading but minor” to “actively deceptive,” and defend their ranking — this opens discussion about intent vs. impact.
Compare to a good graph: Show a well-designed graph on a similar topic and discuss what specific choices make it trustworthy and clear.

title: A Modern Lady Tasting Tea
text: Hypothesis Testing Combinatorics Experimental Design p-values

title: A Modern Lady Tasting Tea
text:
About
This is a modern twist on Ronald Fisher’s famous “Lady Tasting Tea” experiment, the original thought experiment that gave us the foundations of the randomised experiment and the p-value. Instead of milk and tea (feel free to substitute the original if you prefer), this version uses ice and water, which is easier to source, faster to prepare, and just as visually convincing under a projector. Students get a hands-on introduction to combinatorics, the null hypothesis, and just how surprising, or unsurprising, a “perfect score” really is.

title: A Modern Lady Tasting Tea
text: Demonstration

title: A Modern Lady Tasting Tea
text:
Materials

6 identical cups (opaque enough that the order can’t be seen from the side, but see-through from above under the projector)
Ice cubes (2 per cup that gets ice first)
A jug of water
A document camera or projector positioned over the table, so the whole class can watch the cups being prepared
Optional: a “mole” in the room (e.g. a tutor or TA) who can quietly relay the true order to you before you re-enter — see the note in Step 3

title: A Modern Lady Tasting Tea
text:
Step-by-Step Plan

0 (Pre-tasks)

Set up 6 cups on a table positioned under the document camera/projector, so the class (but not you) can see everything from above
Decide in advance how you’ll receive the answer once you step outside (see Step 3)



1 (Setup)
Invite 6 students up to the table. Explain the task:

“In front of you are 6 cups. I’m going to leave the room. While I’m gone, I want 3 of you to each take a cup, place 2 pieces of ice in it, and then pour water in about halfway. I want the other 3 of you to do the same thing, but in the opposite order, i.e., water first, then ice. Do this under the camera so the rest of the class can see exactly what you did. When you’re done, mix up the order of the cups on the table.”



2 (Prediction)
Before you leave the room, ask the rest of the class:

“Once I come back in, my job is to correctly identify which 3 cups had ice first and which 3 had water first, just by looking. If I were purely guessing, what’s the chance I get all 6 correct? What’s the chance I get at least one correct?”

Let students attempt this calculation (or come back to it in Step 5) — it’s a nice lead-in to combinatorics.


3 (Leave the room)
Step outside while the students prepare and mix the cups on camera.






How the “trick” works





This demonstration relies on you actually finding out the order before you walk back in — the surprise is for the audience, not for you. There are two common ways to do this:

A mole in the room: A tutor, TA, or colleague who is in on the demonstration can watch the setup and quietly text you or signal you the order before you re-enter.
A live broadcast: If the class is being recorded or live-streamed (e.g. lecture capture, Zoom), you can watch the feed on your phone from just outside the room while the students set up the cups on camera.

Either way, the “reveal” should still involve genuinely looking at and handling the cups when you return, so it reads as observation rather than being told the answer.





4 (Reveal)
Return to the room. Examine the cups (condensation, temperature, appearance can all serve as your “reasoning” for the audience, even though you already know the order) and announce your classification of each cup as “ice first” or “water first.” Confirm your answers with the students who prepared them.


5 (The Statistics)
Now unpack what just happened:






How many ways can 6 cups be split into two groups of 3?





\[
\binom{6}{3} = \frac{6!}{3!\,3!} = 20
\]
If you were purely guessing which 3 cups were “ice first,” there are 20 equally likely ways to choose them — so the probability of guessing the exact correct split by chance is:
\[
P(\text{all correct}) = \frac{1}{20} = 0.05
\]



Ask the class:

Does a 1-in-20 chance of guessing all 6 correctly feel high or low?
This is exactly the logic behind Fisher’s original experiment and the modern p-value: if someone can correctly sort the cups, and pure guessing would only succeed 5% of the time, do we believe they were guessing?
What if you’d only gotten 5 out of 6 correct — does partial credit change how convinced the class should be?

title: A Modern Lady Tasting Tea
text:
Bonus / Optional:

Can relate this activity to hypothesis testing and Type I error
A few extensions to try:

Formalise the hypotheses: Define \(H_0\): “the taster/observer has no ability to distinguish the cups” vs. \(H_1\): “the taster/observer can distinguish them,” and map the demonstration onto this framework.
Change the design: What happens to the probability of guessing correctly if you used 8 cups (4 and 4) instead of 6? Recalculate \(\binom{8}{4}\) and discuss how experimental design affects the strength of evidence.
Partial credit: Discuss how you’d calculate the probability of getting exactly 2 out of 3 correct by chance, introducing the hypergeometric distribution.
Historical link: Introduce the real Lady Tasting Tea experiment (Muriel Bristol, Ronald Fisher, 1920s Cambridge) and discuss how this simple demonstration led to the development of modern experimental design and significance testing.

title: Jar of Lollies
text: Descriptive Statistics Sampling Estimation Wisdom of Crowds

title: Jar of Lollies
text:
About
This classic “lolly jar” activity is an energetic way to open the semester and immediately involve students in real data collection. By making a simple, intuitive guess, students contribute to a dataset that we can analyse together in real time. The activity introduces the core ideas of descriptive statistics while showing how even everyday judgments form the basis of statistical reasoning.

title: Jar of Lollies
text: Demonstration

title: Jar of Lollies
text:
Materials

One transparent jar filled with small lollies (count them in advance!)
A tool to for students to provide their guess in real time (e.g. Google forms, Poll Everywhere)

title: Jar of Lollies
text:
Step-by-Step Plan

0 (Pre-tasks)

Fill a transparent jar with small lollies. Record how many lollies are in the jar for yourself
Create a question using an online platform (such as Google forms) that only has two questions: (1) Name and (2) Estimate



1 (Setup)
In class (face-to-face or online), hold up the jar and say:

“This jar represents our first dataset of the semester. Your task: estimate how many lollies are inside. Don’t overthink it — just go with your gut.”



2 (Collect data)
Provide students with the link to the online form and get them to fill in their Name and Estimate


3 (Descriptive Stats)
Download the data (Google forms should allow you to export a csv) and show calculations for basic descriptive stats, such as the mean, median, range, variance, sd, etc.


4 (Optional: Plots)
You could generate some plots as a visualisation and link them to certain concepts (e.g. histograms and skewness). You could embed fake responses yourself that are quite extreme to show / talk about outliers.


5 (Reveal)
Show the real count and provide a prize to the winning (or closest guessing) student (if it’s only one correct guess I usually give the whole jar). Multiple winners usually split the prize.

title: Jar of Lollies
text:
Bonus / Optional:

Can relate this activity to sampling
After you’ve revealed the true number, tell students you’ll run a few short experiments to see what happens when we “sample” the data differently. For example:

Small vs. large samples: Randomly select 5 guesses and compute their average. Then select 15 guesses and compute that average. Compare both to the true number — students see that larger samples produce more stable estimates.
Removing outliers: Remove the extreme guesses and recompute the mean and median. Discuss how outliers affect measures of central tendency.
Sampling bias: Ask who sat near the front (closer view of the jar) and whether their guesses were systematically different from those at the back. Introduce the idea of bias and why random sampling matters.
Wisdom of Crowds: If you’re teaching ensemble machine learning, you could consider each individual estimate as a weak learner / model. But by ensembling, you should get an estimate that is quite close to the true value.

title: Class Polls
text: Confidence Intervals Sampling Proportions Live Data

title: Class Polls
text:
About
This activity gets students to generate their own live dataset, again using a simple online form, but this time with two different types of variables:

a numeric response (willingness to pay for coffee) and
a binary response (a light-hearted yes/no question).

Once responses are in, the instructor builds 95% confidence intervals for both live in class, showing students how the CI formula changes depending on whether the underlying variable is continuous or categorical.

title: Class Polls
text: Demonstration

title: Class Polls
text:
Materials

A tool for students to respond in real time (e.g. Google Forms, Poll Everywhere)
A spreadsheet or R session set up in advance to calculate CIs live

title: Class Polls
text:
Step-by-Step Plan

0 (Pre-tasks)

Create a two-question online form:

Numeric: “How much are you willing to pay for a cup of coffee? ($)”
Binary: “Are you wearing fresh underwear today? (Yes/No)”

Test the form yourself and confirm responses export cleanly to a spreadsheet/CSV
Have your stats software (Excel or R) ready with the CI formulas pre-built so you can just paste in live data



1 (Setup)
In class (face-to-face or online), introduce the activity:

“We’re going to collect two very different kinds of data today, one numeric, one binary, and use both to build confidence intervals live. First question is straightforward. Second question… well, the true question is, do we really want to know the answer?”



2 (Collect data)
Share the form link and give students 2–3 minutes to respond to both questions anonymously.


3 (Numeric CI — Coffee Spend)
Download the responses and calculate the 95% CI for the mean amount students are willing to pay.


3 (Numeric CI — Coffee Spend)
Download the responses and calculate the 95% CI for the mean amount students are willing to pay.






Formula: 95% CI for a Mean





\[
\bar{x} \pm t_{\alpha/2, \, n-1} \cdot \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}
\]
where:

\(\bar{x}\) = sample mean
\(s\) = sample standard deviation
\(n\) = sample size
\(t_{\alpha/2, \, n-1}\) = critical value from the t-distribution with \(n-1\) degrees of freedom






4 (Binary CI — Fresh Underwear)
Now calculate the 95% CI for the proportion of students who answered “Yes.”






Formula: 95% CI for a Proportion





\[
\hat{p} \pm z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})}{n}}
\]
where:

\(\hat{p}\) = sample proportion answering “Yes”
\(n\) = sample size
\(z_{\alpha/2} = 1.96\) for 95% confidence






5 (Discuss)
Compare the two intervals as a class:

Why does the coffee CI use a t-distribution while the underwear CI uses a normal approximation?
What happens to each interval’s width as n increases?
What would happen to the binary CI if p̂ were very close to 0 or 1 (e.g. almost everyone says “Yes”)? This is a good moment to mention that the normal approximation breaks down in that case, and alternatives like the Wilson or Clopper-Pearson interval exist.

title: Class Polls
text:
Bonus / Optional:

Can relate this activity to sample size and margin of error more broadly
A few extensions to try:

Shrinking the CI: Ask “what sample size would we need to halve this margin of error?” and calculate it live.
Compare subgroups: If you collected any grouping variable (e.g. year level), compute separate CIs for each group and compare.
Interval interpretation: Poll students on what they think “95% confidence” means, then correct common misconceptions (it’s not “95% probability the true value is in this interval”).
Method comparison: For the binary variable, compute the Wilson interval alongside the normal-approximation interval and discuss when they diverge.

title: Skittle Science
text: Chi-Square Test Goodness of Fit Categorical Data Expected vs Observed

title: Skittle Science
text:
About
This activity uses a large bag of Skittles to test a simple assumption most students take for granted: that each colour is equally likely. Before opening the bag, students guess the colour distribution and submit a prediction, with a prize for whoever gets closest (the instructor can decide how this works). Once the bag is counted, the class discovers whether the colours really are split evenly — and uses a chi-square goodness-of-fit test to formally check whether the observed counts are consistent with an equal (“uniform”) distribution, or whether the deviation is too large to be chance.






Note



If you want to do this as a trick, then open (carefully) and count this yourself first. And write down the exact distribution. Then place the skittles back in, try to seal it in a way that looks like it has not been opened. When performing the demonstration, open from that original location.

title: Skittle Science
text: Demonstration

title: Skittle Science
text:
Materials

One large bag of Skittles (the bigger the better — more candy means a more reliable test)
A tool for students to submit their distribution guesses (e.g. Google Forms)
A way to sort and count the Skittles by colour in front of the class (paper plates, cups, or just piles on a table under a document camera)
A small prize for the closest guess
A spreadsheet or R session set up to calculate the chi-square statistic live

title: Skittle Science
text:
Step-by-Step Plan

0 (Pre-tasks)

Buy one large bag of Skittles — don’t open it or count it in advance, so the reveal is genuine
Set up a short prediction form asking students to guess the percentage split across the standard colours (e.g. Red, Orange, Yellow, Green, Purple)
Decide on your prize and how you’ll score “closest” guess (see the callout in Step 4)



1 (Setup)
Hold up the unopened bag and ask the class:

“If I open this bag and count every Skittle by colour, what distribution would you expect? Equal numbers of each colour, or something else?”

Let the class debate briefly before moving on.


2 (Collect Predictions)
Have each student submit their guess for the colour distribution — e.g. as five percentages that sum to 100%, or as a ranked order from “most common” to “least common” colour if you want a simpler task.

“Whoever’s guess ends up closest to the real distribution wins the prize — so think carefully.”



3 (Open and Count)
Open the bag and sort the Skittles into piles by colour under the document camera, counting each pile out loud as you go so the whole class can follow along. Record the final counts on the board.


4 (Reveal the Winner)
Compare each student’s prediction to the actual counts and announce the winner.






Scoring the guesses





A simple way to score “closest” is to sum the absolute difference between each student’s guessed percentage and the actual percentage for every colour, then award the prize to whoever has the smallest total difference. This also doubles as a nice lead-in to talking about error/residuals before you even get to the chi-square formula.





5 (Set Up the Hypotheses)
Before running any test, formalise what you’re actually checking:
\[
H_0: \text{All colours are equally likely } \left(p_{\text{red}} = p_{\text{orange}} = p_{\text{yellow}} = p_{\text{green}} = p_{\text{purple}} = \frac{1}{5}\right)
\]
\[
H_1: \text{At least one colour's true proportion differs from } \frac{1}{5}
\]


6 (Calculate Expected Counts)
If the null hypothesis were true, each colour should make up an equal share of the total. Calculate the expected count per colour:
\[
E_i = \frac{n}{k}
\]
where \(n\) is the total number of Skittles counted and \(k\) is the number of colour categories (typically 5).


7 (Calculate the Chi-Square Statistic)
Compare the observed counts (\(O_i\)) from Step 3 to the expected counts (\(E_i\)) from Step 6:
\[
\chi^2 = \sum_{i=1}^{k} \frac{(O_i - E_i)^2}{E_i}
\]
Walk through the calculation live, colour by colour, building the sum on the board so students see exactly how much each colour contributes to the total statistic.


8 (Compare to the Critical Value)
Compare your calculated \(\chi^2\) statistic to the critical value from a chi-square distribution with \(k - 1\) degrees of freedom (4, for 5 colours) at \(\alpha = 0.05\).






Degrees of Freedom





\[
df = k - 1
\]
For 5 colours, \(df = 4\). Look up (or calculate) the critical value \(\chi^2_{0.05, \, 4}\), and compare it to your calculated statistic — if your statistic exceeds the critical value, reject \(H_0\).





9 (Conclude)
Discuss the result as a class: was the distribution actually equal, or did the test detect a real imbalance? Which colour(s) contributed the most to the chi-square statistic, and does that match what the class predicted back in Step 2?

title: Skittle Science
text:
Bonus / Optional:

Can relate this activity to sample size and statistical power
A few extensions to try:

Pool the class’s bags: If multiple students each bring their own small bag, pool all the counts together and compare the chi-square result using the full pooled sample versus just your one large bag — larger \(n\) typically makes it easier to detect a real deviation.
Compare bag sizes/brands: If time allows, repeat with a different bag size or a different candy brand entirely, and discuss whether the “equal distribution” assumption holds up across different production batches.
Effect size: Beyond just significance, calculate Cramér’s V to discuss how large the imbalance actually is, not just whether it’s statistically detectable.
Link to independence testing: Discuss how this differs from a chi-square test of independence (e.g. testing whether colour distribution differs between two different bags) versus the goodness-of-fit test used here (comparing one bag’s distribution to a fixed theoretical expectation).

title: Contagious Yawns
text: Correlation Linear Regression Data Collection Psychology of Empathy

title: Contagious Yawns
text:
About
Contagious yawning has long been studied as a possible marker of empathy — the idea being that people who are more attuned to others’ emotional and physical states are more likely to “catch” a yawn. This activity turns that idea into a live regression exercise: students watch a short yawning video and record the exact moment (if any) they yawned, then complete a short empathy questionnaire. The two measurements: time-to-yawn and empathy score become the dataset for a hands-on correlation and regression analysis.

title: Contagious Yawns
text: Demonstration

title: Contagious Yawns
text:
Materials

A short video of people yawning, with a visible on-screen counter/timer (see Step 2)
Access to an online empathy questionnaire (see Step 3)
A tool for students to submit their data in real time (e.g. Google Forms)
A stats package (Excel, R, or similar) to run the correlation and regression live

title: Contagious Yawns
text:
Step-by-Step Plan

0 (Pre-tasks)

Preview the yawning video yourself and confirm the on-screen counter is clearly visible throughout
Set up a short online form with three fields: (1) Name/ID, (2) Time (in seconds) at which they yawned, or “Did not yawn,” and (3) their empathy score from the questionnaire
Test the empathy questionnaire link yourself and note roughly how long it takes to complete (so you can budget class time)



1 (Setup)
In class, explain the activity without revealing the hypothesis in too much detail up front:

“I’m going to play a short video. Just watch it naturally. There’s a counter in the corner — if you yawn at any point, note down the number on the counter at that exact moment. If you don’t yawn at all, that’s fine too, just note that down.”



2 (Watch and Record — Predictor Variable)
Play the yawning video. You may want to stop the video earlier if your class time is short.
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=AJXX4vF6Zh0
Immediately afterward, have students record:

The counter value at the moment they yawned, or
“Did not yawn” if they didn’t

This is your predictor variable (\(X\)) — time-to-yawn (or a large/undefined value for non-yawners, discussed further in the Bonus section).


3 (Empathy Questionnaire — Outcome Variable)
Direct students to complete the empathy questionnaire and record their score. This is your outcome variable (\(Y\)).
Have students submit both values through your form.


4 (Explore the Data)
Download the combined dataset and start with a scatterplot of empathy score (y-axis) against time-to-yawn (x-axis), restricted to students who yawned.

Scatterplot (concept)What to look for


Plot empathy score against yawn time. Ask the class: does there seem to be a pattern? Do earlier yawners cluster toward higher or lower empathy scores?



Direction: Does empathy tend to go up or down as yawn-time increases?
Strength: Are the points tightly clustered around a line, or scattered widely?
Outliers: Any students who yawned very early or very late with an unexpected empathy score?






5 (Correlation)
Calculate the correlation coefficient between yawn time and empathy score. I usually use software, but you can do it manually as well:






Formula: Pearson Correlation Coefficient





\[
r = \frac{\sum (x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y})}{\sqrt{\sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2 \sum (y_i - \bar{y})^2}}
\]
where \(x_i\) is each student’s yawn time and \(y_i\) is their empathy score.
\(r\) ranges from \(-1\) to \(1\). A negative \(r\) here would suggest that earlier yawning is associated with higher empathy — consistent with the contagious-yawning-as-empathy hypothesis.





6 (Simple Linear Regression)
Fit a regression line predicting empathy score from yawn time. Again, software is a huge time saver.






Formula: Simple Linear Regression





\[
\hat{Y} = b_0 + b_1 X
\]
\[
b_1 = \frac{\sum (x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y})}{\sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2}
\qquad
b_0 = \bar{y} - b_1 \bar{x}
\]
where:

\(b_1\) = the estimated change in empathy score for each additional second before yawning
\(b_0\) = the predicted empathy score for a (hypothetical) yawn time of zero seconds




Plot the fitted line over the scatterplot from Step 4 and discuss what the slope means in plain terms: for every extra second before a student yawns, how much does their predicted empathy score change?


7 (Interpret and Critique)
Discuss as a class:

How strong was the correlation, really? Is it statistically meaningful given the sample size (your class)?
What does \(R^2\) tell us about how much of the variation in empathy scores is “explained” by yawn time?
What are the limitations of this design? (Small sample, self-reported yawning, single time-point, potential confounders like tiredness or attention)

title: Contagious Yawns
text:
Bonus / Optional:

Can relate this activity to confounding variables and the difference between correlation and causation
A few extensions to try:

Handling non-yawners: Discuss how to treat students who didn’t yawn at all — should they be excluded, or coded as a large value/right-censored? This is a nice, gentle introduction to the idea of censored data.
Multiple regression: If you collect additional variables (e.g. hours of sleep, whether they watched a screen recently), extend the model to multiple predictors and discuss how each new variable changes the interpretation of the others.
Correlation ≠ causation: Ask the class to brainstorm alternative explanations for any observed relationship — e.g. more attentive/empathetic students may simply have been watching the video more closely, rather than empathy directly causing yawning.
Residual analysis: Plot the residuals from the regression model and discuss what a “good” residual plot should look like (no clear pattern) versus a problematic one (funnel shape, curve).

title: 10 Second Challenge
text: Residuals Normal Distribution Measurement Error Bias vs. Variance

title: 10 Second Challenge
text:
About
Students try to stop a timer as close as possible to exactly 10.00 seconds. Each attempt records a signed error (observed time minus target time), and after several attempts, the app summarises the mean error, best absolute error, and standard deviation of times. This is a simple but effective hook for residuals: every attempt’s error is exactly analogous to a residual in a regression model — the gap between an observed value and a “true” target. With enough attempts pooled across the class, the errors tend to scatter in a roughly bell-shaped pattern around zero, giving a hands-on way to introduce the normal distribution of errors, and to separate two very different kinds of “being wrong”: a biased timer (consistently early or late — a non-zero mean error) versus a noisy one (highly variable, but centred correctly — a large standard deviation with a mean error near zero).

text:
General questions

After several attempts, were your errors mostly positive, mostly negative, or a mix of both? What would that pattern suggest about your internal sense of timing?
What’s the difference between having a mean error far from zero versus having a large standard deviation of your times? Which one describes “consistently wrong,” and which describes “unpredictable”?
If your very first attempt happened to be exact (0.00s error), would that tell you much about how good you are at this task? Why or why not?
As a class, pool everyone’s errors together and look at the shape of the distribution. Does it look roughly symmetric and bell-shaped around zero, or is it skewed one way?
In a regression model, a “residual” is the gap between what a model predicts and what actually happened. How is your error on this task similar to a residual? How is it different?
If someone was consistently early by about 0.5 seconds on every attempt, would practicing more make them more accurate, more precise, both, or neither? What would actually need to change?
Where else in real life do we see this same distinction between a biased measurement process and a noisy one (e.g. a scale that’s always off by the same amount, versus one that gives a different reading every time you step on it)?

title: Colour Game
text: Permutation Test Bootstrap Between-Subjects Design Resampling

title: Colour Game
text:
About
This app is a fast-paced colour-matching game, structurally similar to the Stack Game but with a different task and a different outcome measure. As before, are assigned to one of two conditions before playing: Control, the standard game with no interruptions, or Distraction, where notification-style pop-ups appear periodically during play. Note: if following on from the Stack game, you could switch groups.
Everyone plays the same underlying game, only the presence of distractions differs between groups, making this another clean between-subjects comparison - this time used to introduce resampling-based hypothesis testing rather than the standard t-test. Instead of relying on the t-distribution, students use the class’s own data to build a permutation test (repeatedly shuffling group labels to see how extreme the observed group difference really is) and a bootstrap (resampling within each group to build a confidence interval for the difference in means). Both methods let students see hypothesis testing as a simulation problem rather than a formula lookup, useful groundwork before moving to more complex parametric tests.

title: Colour Game
text:
Permutation Test
Once the class’s scores are compiled into two groups (Control, Distraction), calculate the observed difference in means:
\[
\hat{\Delta} = \bar{x}_{\text{control}} - \bar{x}_{\text{distraction}}
\]
A permutation test asks: if group membership had no real effect, how often would a difference this large (or larger) show up just from randomly relabelling who was in which group?

scores <- c(control_scores, distraction_scores)
group  <- c(rep("control", length(control_scores)), rep("distraction", length(distraction_scores)))

observed_diff <- mean(control_scores) - mean(distraction_scores)

n_perm <- 10000
perm_diffs <- numeric(n_perm)

set.seed(1)
for (i in 1:n_perm) {
  shuffled <- sample(group)
  perm_diffs[i] <- mean(scores[shuffled == "control"]) - mean(scores[shuffled == "distraction"])
}

p_value <- mean(abs(perm_diffs) >= abs(observed_diff))

Plot a histogram of perm_diffs with a vertical line at observed_diff — this is a highly visual way for students to see exactly what a p-value represents: the proportion of the shuffled world that looks at least as extreme as what was actually observed.

title: Colour Game
text:
Bootstrap Confidence Interval
Rather than testing a hypothesis, the bootstrap estimates a range of plausible values for the true difference in means, by resampling within each group (with replacement) many times.

n_boot <- 10000
boot_diffs <- numeric(n_boot)

set.seed(1)
for (i in 1:n_boot) {
  boot_control     <- sample(control_scores, replace = TRUE)
  boot_distraction <- sample(distraction_scores, replace = TRUE)
  boot_diffs[i] <- mean(boot_control) - mean(boot_distraction)
}

ci <- quantile(boot_diffs, c(0.025, 0.975))

Compare this bootstrap confidence interval to the observed difference from the permutation test — do they tell a consistent story? Ask the class: does the interval include zero? What would that mean if it did?

title: Colour Game
text:
General questions

Why do we shuffle the group labels rather than the scores themselves in a permutation test? What would happen if we shuffled something else?
The permutation test and the bootstrap both involve “resampling,” but they answer different questions. Can you describe, in your own words, what each one is actually trying to tell you?
If the permutation test’s p-value came out just above or just below 0.05, how confident should the class be in that conclusion? What would you want to know before trusting it?
Why might resampling-based methods like these be more intuitive (or more trustworthy) to a beginner than a formula-based t-test, even though they’re often testing a similar hypothesis?
If you ran the permutation test again with a different random seed, would you expect the p-value to change? By how much, roughly?
As with the Stack Game, students weren’t randomly assigned to Control vs. Distraction. How might that affect how much we can trust either the permutation test or bootstrap result here?

title: MontyHall
text:
About
The Monty Hall problem is one of the most famous (and most argued-about) puzzles in probability. Students are almost always confident that staying or switching makes no difference — after all, with two doors left, isn’t it 50/50? This interactive app lets students test that intuition directly: they play the game themselves, repeatedly, and watch a live crosstab build up showing how often “stay” wins versus how often “switch” wins. The gap between intuition and the empirical result is what makes this activity land — no lecture is as convincing as students’ own accumulating data.

title: RockPaperScissors
text:
About
Students play 10 rounds of Rock Paper Scissors against the computer, watching their running score plotted live as they go. With only 10 games, results swing wildly — a player can be up 4 points after 5 games and end up losing, purely from the small sample size. This is a great hook for discussing why small samples are noisy and unreliable estimators of a “true” underlying rate, and why the Law of Large Numbers only kicks in once you play many, many more rounds. As a twist, the computer opponent isn’t purely random — it quietly adapts based on the outcome of the previous round — which opens up a second discussion thread on detecting non-randomness and pattern-seeking behaviour once students start noticing (or suspecting) a pattern in the computer’s choices.

General questions

After 10 games, did your final score feel like a fair reflection of your actual skill against the computer, or could it easily have gone the other way with a bit of luck?
If you played another 10 games right now, would you expect a similar result, a completely different one, or something in between? Why?
How many games do you think you’d need to play before your win rate started to “settle down” and reliably reflect the true probabilities involved?
Did you notice any pattern in the computer’s choices as you played? If you suspected a pattern, how would you go about testing whether it was real or just your imagination?
If a friend told you they’d won 8 out of 10 games against the computer and concluded “I’m just better at reading the computer,” what would you want to know before you believed them?
As a class, compare everyone’s final scores. Do they all cluster around a similar result, or is there a wide spread? What does that spread tell you about how much weight to put on any one person’s 10-game outcome?
Where else in everyday life do people draw big conclusions from a small number of outcomes (a few good trades, a short winning streak, a handful of “lucky” days) that might really just be normal randomness?

title: Stack Game
text:
About
This app is a fast-paced block-stacking game with a hidden research design baked in. Before playing, the instructor will allocate students into one of trwo conditions: Control, the standard game with no interruptions, or Distraction, where a new notification-style pop-up (a text, a low battery warning, a calling gem) appears after every successful stack. Everyone plays the same game with the same mechanics — the only thing that differs between groups is whether they’re being pulled away from the task with simulated phone notifications. This is a clean, self-contained between-subjects design: students self-select (or are randomly assigned by the instructor) into one of two independent groups, and their final scores become the outcome variable for a live hypothesis test comparing means.

Before playing, did you expect the distraction messages to affect your score much? Did the actual experience match that expectation?
If the instructor let students freely choose which group (Control or Distraction) to join, could that cause a problem when comparing the two groups afterward? What would you suggest instead?
Why is it important that both groups play the exact same game, with only the distractions differing? What would go wrong if the Distraction group also had a different game mechanic?
As a class, compare the average scores of the Control group and the Distraction group. Does there appear to be a difference? How confident are you that this difference (if any) reflects a real effect, rather than just random variation between two groups of different people?
Some students might get distracted by a notification and actually play better out of a spike in adrenaline or focus. How would that possibility affect how we interpret the results?
Outside of this game, where else does a “distraction condition vs. control condition” comparison show up in real research or everyday life (e.g. studying with music on vs. off, driving while texting)?
If this experiment were repeated with a much larger class, would you expect the difference between groups to become clearer, or would it stay just as uncertain? Why?

title: Surveyor Builder
text: Estimation Sampling Bias Survey Design Standard Error

title: Surveyor Builder
text:
About
In this app, students build their own field surveyor by allocating skill points across five traits: Charm, Intelligence, Efficiency, Local Knowledge, and Persistence, before sending them out to estimate the average weekly household income of a 10,000-household town. Only the instructor knows the true population mean ($1,250); students never see it directly, only the single sample estimate their surveyor comes back with. Because each trait trades off differently (e.g. Charm boosts response rate, Intelligence reduces measurement error, Local Knowledge reduces coverage bias), different point allocations produce systematically different, and sometimes very wrong, estimates, even though every student is sampling from the exact same town. This makes for a great class-wide comparison: once everyone reveals their estimate, the spread across the room becomes the lesson itself, showing how response bias, coverage bias, and measurement error can each quietly drag an estimate away from the truth, even without anyone doing anything “wrong.”

General questions

Why might two students with the exact same total number of skill points end up with very different estimates, just from allocating those points differently?
If you had to guess blind, which single trait do you think matters most for getting an accurate estimate — and why?
What’s the difference between a surveyor who gets a high response rate but poor coverage, versus one who gets low response rate but excellent coverage? Which sounds worse to you, and why?
Once the true mean is revealed, was your estimate too high or too low? Can you explain why, based on the trait choices you made?
If you could only pick one trait to max out and ignore the rest, which would you choose, and what would you expect to go wrong as a result?
As a class, look at everyone’s final estimates together. Do they cluster around the true value, or are they scattered all over the place? What does that tell you about how much you should trust any one person’s single estimate in real life?
Real government surveys (like the Census) spend enormous amounts of money trying to maximise coverage and response rate. Based on what you just experienced, why might that expense be worth it?

title: Research
text:
Beyond the hooks and activities on this site, I’m also genuinely interested in the broader question of what makes statistics education actually work, e.g.

why some explanations land and others don’t?
why a well-timed demonstration can shift how a whole cohort engages with a topic?
how we might measure that more rigorously than just “the class seemed to enjoy it.”

If any of that sparks your curiosity, there’s a good chance there’s a research project in it.
Statistics education is a surprisingly under-explored space, especially compared to how much energy goes into the statistics itself. There’s real scope for projects looking at engagement and retention, the effectiveness of interactive versus demonstration-based teaching, how students’ confidence in a topic shifts before and after a hook-style activity, or even building and evaluating new hooks of your own from the ground up. Some of this could be quite data-driven, running one of the apps on this site across a few cohorts and analysing what actually happened , while other angles might be more qualitative, digging into student reflections and classroom observations.
I’d particularly love to hear from students looking for an honours, minor thesis, or postgraduate research project, but honestly, I’m happy to chat with anyone who has a genuine interest in this space, regardless of where you’re at. You don’t need a fully-formed proposal to reach out. A rough idea, or even just “I liked this website and want to do something related to it,” is more than enough of a starting point. Some of the best projects start as loose ideas that get shaped properly once we sit down and talk them through.
If this all sounds interesting, drop me an email at minh.huynh1@monash.edu and we can set up a time to discuss. I’m happy to talk through possible directions, how a project might be scoped, and what it would actually look like day to day.
